n: This verse wraps up the tribal genealogies and bluntly states why Judah went into exile: unfaithfulness. Yet the careful records show that God’s people still had an identity worth preserving.

f.g: Registered by family records, establishing each person’s tribe and place.

f.w: carried away to Babylon for their transgression

n: The chronicler now lists those who resettled their towns after the exile: lay Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants. Much of this list parallels Nehemiah 11.

f.g: “Those given”—temple servants who assisted the Levites.

n: Families from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem. Including northern tribes shows the chronicler’s hope that “all Israel” belongs together.
Uthai led a family from Judah’s Pharez line—the same line as David.
The Shilonites, probably descendants of Judah’s son Shelah, are represented by Asaiah.

f.g: Probably “Shelanites,” descendants of Shelah (Numbers 26:20), rather than people from Shiloh.

n: Zerah’s descendants, the third branch of Judah, numbered 690. All three branches of Judah were represented in the restored city.
Benjamite families in Jerusalem are listed with their ancestry.
More Benjamite family heads, each identified by several generations of ancestors.

f.g: A very common name after the exile, meaning “restored” or “recompensed.”

n: The Benjamites in Jerusalem numbered 956 family heads and relatives.

f.g: Leading family heads.

n: The priestly families begin with Jedaiah and Jehoiarib, names that match two of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized.
Azariah, descended from Zadok, was the chief officer of the temple—showing the high priestly line continued after exile.

f.w: the ruler of the house of God
f.g: Chief officer or overseer of the temple.

n: Other priests are listed from the families of Pashur and Immer, both known from Jeremiah’s time.
There were 1,760 priests—capable men ready to serve in God’s house.

f.g: Strong, capable men, fit for demanding temple service.

n: The Levites begin with Shemaiah of Merari’s branch.
Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, led the thanksgiving in worship after the return.
Obadiah, a descendant of Jeduthun, and Berechiah, who lived near Netophah, were also Levite musicians.

f.g: People of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem where many Levite singers lived (Nehemiah 12:28).

n: The gatekeepers are named, led by Shallum.

f.g: Gatekeepers or doorkeepers, not carriers.

n: Shallum’s family had long guarded the King’s Gate on the east side of the temple.

f.g: Until now; up to this time.

n: These Korahite gatekeepers carried on a duty their ancestors had performed since the wilderness tabernacle—guarding the entrance to God’s dwelling.

f.g: Here meaning the camp of Israel around the tabernacle.

n: Phinehas once supervised these guards, and “the LORD was with him”—a blessing the chronicler hopes for every faithful servant.
Zechariah guarded the entrance of the tent of meeting in David’s time.
There were 212 gatekeepers, registered in their villages. Their roles traced back to arrangements made by David and Samuel.

f.g: An older title for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9).
In their assigned, trusted position.

n: These families supervised the temple gates in rotating shifts.

f.g: In shifts or watches.

n: Gatekeepers were stationed on all four sides of the temple.
Relatives from the villages came in to serve week-long shifts, rotating regularly.

f.g: Every seven days—a weekly rotation, like the priests’ courses (Luke 1:8-9).

n: Four chief gatekeepers held permanent positions and oversaw the storerooms and treasuries.

f.g: Storerooms for offerings, tithes and sacred items.

n: They lived around the temple and opened its doors every morning—a faithful daily duty.

f.g: They were responsible for guarding it.

n: Some kept track of the sacred vessels, counting them carefully as they were brought in and out.

f.g: By count; by number.

n: Others managed temple supplies: flour, wine, oil, incense and spices for offerings.

f.g: A fragrant resin burned as incense.

n: Only priests mixed the sacred anointing oil and incense, as the law of Moses required.

f.w: made the ointment of the spices

n: Mattithiah was in charge of baking the flat cakes for grain offerings.

f.w: the things that were made in the pans
f.g: Baked grain offerings (Leviticus 2:5; 1 Chronicles 23:29).

n: Kohathites prepared the showbread each Sabbath—twelve loaves set before the Lord, one for each tribe.

f.g: “Bread of the Presence,” twelve loaves kept on a table in the holy place.

n: The Levite musicians lived in temple rooms and were freed from other duties, because they served day and night.
These Levite family heads lived in Jerusalem.

f.g: Living near the temple allowed them to serve continually.

n: The chronicler repeats Saul’s family tree from chapter 8, here as a bridge into the story of Saul’s death in chapter 10.
Jehiel’s sons, now including Ner, Saul’s grandfather.

f.g: Saul’s grandfather; also the father of Abner, Saul’s general (1 Samuel 14:50).

n: The rest of Jehiel’s sons, including Mikloth.

f.g: Called Zacher in 1 Chronicles 8:31.

n: Mikloth’s family lived in Jerusalem near their relatives.

f.g: Called Shimeah in 1 Chronicles 8:32.

n: Saul and his sons are named again, preparing the reader for their deaths at Mount Gilboa.
Jonathan’s son Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) and grandson Micah carried Jonathan’s line forward.
Micah’s four sons.

f.g: Called Tarea in 1 Chronicles 8:35.

n: Saul’s line continues through several generations.

f.g: Called Jehoadah in 1 Chronicles 8:36.

n: The descendants continue to Azel.

f.g: Called Rapha in 1 Chronicles 8:37.

n: Azel’s six sons end the list. The chronicler is now ready to begin his narrative with Saul’s fall and David’s rise.
